## Why Compare Two Groups?

<br>

Most interesting questions are [comparative]{.gold}:

<br>

- Does taking aspirin daily reduce the rate of heart attacks?
- Is the graduation rate different for transfer vs. first-year admits?
- Do handwritten notes lead to better exam pass rates than laptop notes?

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
The parameter of interest: [$p_1 - p_2$]{.teal style="font-size: 1.2em;"}
:::

---

## The Setup

<br>

Two independent random samples:

<br>

| | Group 1 | Group 2 |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| Sample size | $n_1$ | $n_2$ |
| Successes | $x_1$ | $x_2$ |
| Sample proportion | $\hat{p}_1 = x_1/n_1$ | $\hat{p}_2 = x_2/n_2$ |

<br>

[Goal:]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} make inferences about $p_1 - p_2$ using $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$

<br>

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.65);"}
*Same logic as one-proportion inference --- the tools just get a second subscript*
:::

---

## One-Prop CI

[What it does:]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} estimate the true proportion $p$ by building a range of plausible values around $\hat{p}$

$$\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$

SE uses [$\hat{p}$]{.gold} because we're [estimating]{.teal} --- we don't know $p$

---

## Two-Prop CI

[What it does:]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} estimate the difference $p_1 - p_2$ by building a range of plausible values around $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$

$$(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z_{\alpha/2} \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}$$

Each group keeps its own $\hat{p}$ in the SE --- just like one-prop CI uses $\hat{p}$

<br>

[Is 0 in the interval?]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} &ensp;All positive → $p_1 > p_2$. &ensp;All negative → $p_1 < p_2$. &ensp;Contains 0 → can't conclude a difference at this confidence level.

---

## One-Prop HT

[What it does:]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} test whether $p$ equals a claimed value $p_0$

- $H_0$: $p = p_0$ &ensp;(the claim is true)
- $H_1$: $p \neq p_0$ &ensp;(or $<$ or $>$)

$$z_0 = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}$$

SE uses [$p_0$]{.gold} because we [assume]{.teal} $H_0$ is true

---

## Two-Prop HT: The Pooled Proportion

<br>

$H_0$: $p_1 = p_2$ --- under the null, we believe the two groups have the [same]{.gold} true proportion

<br>

If they share the same $p$, our best estimate of that common value uses [all the data]{.teal}:

$$\hat{p} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}$$

This is called the [pooled proportion]{.gold} --- we combine ("pool") both samples into one because $H_0$ says there's no difference between them

---

## Two-Prop HT: Test Statistic

<br>

$$z_0 = \frac{(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}}$$

where $\hat{p} = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2}$ (the pooled proportion)

<br>

- Same p-value logic as one-prop (left / right / two-tailed)
- Same conclusion language: "sufficient / not sufficient evidence that..."

---

<br>

```{=html}
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">

</table>
```

<br>

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
[The formula is always $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$]{.teal style="font-weight: 600;"} --- the reasoning about [which $p$]{.gold} changes
:::
